title: Beneath our human shallows
author: James Dinneen
bodyHtml:
When Soviet engineers began to drain the Aral Sea in the 1960s, they could hardly foresee the scale on which their handiwork would alter the planet. The goal was to irrigate large areas of what is now Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan to grow cotton, part of a utopian project stretching back to czarist Russia to civilise the ‘backward’ regions of central Asia. Achieving this meant diverting most of the two rivers that fed the Aral Sea, which was then the fourth largest lake in the world, larger than Lake Michigan. The engineers didn’t mean to empty it, but that was the outcome: the loss of input from the rivers, along with drought, caused nearly 90 per cent of its area to dry up over the next several decades. Today, abandoned fishing boats sit on the empty expanse as evidence of one of the 20th century’s largest environmental catastrophes.

But the consequences of this event were not limited to the surface. The disappearance of around 1,000 cubic km of water provoked a rebound response all the way down in the upper mantle. Without that mass of water pressing down, the crust began to rise. In 2025, the geophysicist Teng Wang at Peking University and colleagues used satellites to measure the rate of uplift – known as isostatic adjustment or the ‘mattress effect’. They found an average rise across the former sea since 2016 of about 7 mm per year. Their models suggest that could occur only if viscous rocks in the upper mantle were ‘creeping’ into the space beneath the crust – as far as 190 km below the surface.

This is, as far as I’ve been able to determine, the deepest effect that a single human act has had on Earth. Our deliberate subterranean activities don’t come close. The deepest mine reaches no more than 4 km beneath the surface in South Africa. The deepest hole ever drilled, the Kola ‘Superdeep’ Borehole in northern Russia – another Russian engineering megaproject – punctures just 12 km down. Decades of scientific efforts to drill a ‘mohole’ into the mantle by boring into the thinnest parts of oceanic crust have been unsuccessful.

From that standpoint, the fact that a man-made environmental disaster altered the upper mantle is a shocking illustration of the scale of the planetary transformations that mark the Anthropocene – the age in which humans are supposedly the central geological force on Earth. It would also seem to suggest that human activity could be affecting Earth’s interior in other ways. What does the Anthropocene look like from below?

I’ve been thinking about this question of late because of a book I’m writing about the deep Earth, both the role it plays in making a habitable planet and how scientists have investigated its secrets. While human influence on Earth has certainly pushed deeper in the Anthropocene, what has become clear to me is that, from the planet’s perspective, we’re actually quite a shallow species. Our future scraping by up here on the surface depends on coming to terms with that.

For the most part, debates about the Anthropocene have focused more on when it started rather than where its influence extends. Did it begin at the dawn of agriculture? The Industrial Revolution? Or the mid-20th century, when nuclear weapons testing imprinted rocks worldwide? Ultimately, disagreement over whether this epochal change could be tied to a single discrete marker in the strata led to its rejection as an official new chapter in the geological record. But the term continues to be widely used as a catch-all for the planetary impacts the industrialised world now has on Earth, including those that extend increasingly far beneath the surface.

For instance, in a study from 2024, a group of geoscientists led by Grant Ferguson at the University of Saskatchewan estimated the volume of fluid moving through the subsurface due to global oil and gas production and mining, and found this human-caused flux now exceeds the total natural flow of groundwater deeper than 500 metres. This suggests that, as far as half a kilometre down, humans are, at the moment, the main event. The most significant consequence of pumping up all those ancient hydrocarbons is climate change – this is a shift of carbon from the lithosphere to the atmosphere far outpacing the largest super-eruptions in Earth’s history. There are also consequences within the subsurface itself. The movement of all that fluid has also induced earthquakes in some cases. The researchers suggested it may also have effects on the microbial ecosystems that thrive within the vast ‘deep biosphere’ that lives within the crust, although, like many things about this deep life, the nature of those impacts is unknown.

This isn’t just a picture of fossil fuel extraction, though. The researchers anticipated this deep fluid flux would see a substantial acceleration with a green transition away from fossil fuels, given the expansion of mining required for minerals to build batteries, wind and solar energy – already mines are getting bigger and digging deeper. Geothermal energy, geologic hydrogen extraction and projects sequestering CO2 all tap into the underground as well. This transition could leave behind its own anthropogenic signature much deeper in the rock record than other candidate markers of the Anthropocene. In 2025, for example, an experimental CO2 storage project in Washington state injecting fluids more than 800 m underground found they had created ‘anthropogenic carbonates’ that included crystalline structures not found in nature. Given that the nascent CO2 removal industry envisions eventually sequestering billions of tonnes of CO2 in the subsurface each year, it’s not impossible to imagine this layer expanding, leaving behind a strange, carbon-rich unconformity in the basement rock to puzzle geologists of the distant future.

The great majority of Earth has no clue that humans exist, and probably never will

Even these deep flows, however, are dwarfed by groundwater extraction from shallower aquifers, which continues at a rate of around 1,000 cubic km per year – the equivalent of sucking a whole Aral Sea out of the ground every 12 months. This has had local impacts in many of the world’s most important agricultural regions, driving land subsidence and forcing farmers to dig ever deeper wells and use ever more energy to irrigate crops. It has also had planetary-scale impacts. One study estimated the global redistribution of mass due to groundwater pumping between 1993 and 2010 shifted the location of Earth’s axis of rotation by nearly a metre. A 2025 paper found that freshwater running off the continents due to groundwater extraction now contributes more to sea level rise than the melting of the glaciers and ice sheets. Humans are pulling water and carbon up to the surface faster than natural processes can keep up.

There are other ways the Anthropocene could reach even deeper than our drills, pumps and excavators. As with the isostatic uplift underneath the Aral Sea, a total retreat of the glaciers and ice sheets in response to human-caused climate change could shift mass around in a way that produces an even deeper mantle response than the Soviet engineers triggered in the 1960s. This could contribute to the isostatic readjustment underway since the end of the last glacial period, and alter relative sea level along many coastlines. There’s reason to think these climate-driven changes to the solid Earth could spur volcanism and earthquakes too. One study found ice loss in Antarctica could relieve pressure on underground magma chambers beneath the ice, increasing the rate of eruptions, which could in turn accelerate melting from below.

Looking much further out in time, tens of millions of years ahead, one could imagine a faint human signature will descend further down as today’s oceanic crust is subducted into the mantle. This would carry with it all the human refuse accumulated within the marine sediment piled atop the slab – the eroded soils and coal ash, the microplastics and plutonium, the fossil CO2 of the past three-ish centuries shifted from the subsurface to the atmosphere and back again. I imagine most of this would be melted and remixed, diluted by the far vaster volume of the mantle. It’s possible some faint isotopic whiff of humans remains detectable when a bit of that anthrosediment is remobilised out of a volcanic arc in a few million years. Conceivably, hundreds of millions of years from now, a few bits of the Anthropocene might even make it down with the slab all the way to the edge of the core, laid to rest within the tectonic graveyard of the lowermost mantle nearly 3,000 km down.

Such examples of humans pushing ever deeper might seem to suggest that the Anthropocene matters for the deep Earth too. But I think the overall effect is the opposite: it makes the planet seem bigger and us humans smaller. Unlike the transformations of the surface, none of these human signatures represent transformations or influence over the much grander processes of Earth’s interior. Even the Aral Sea drainage, which reached 190 km down, is nothing from the deep Earth’s perspective: less than 3 per cent of the way to the planet’s centre. The great majority of Earth – down through the expanse of the upper and lower mantle, through the liquid outer core, and the solid inner core – has no clue that humans exist, and probably never will. The past few decades of geoscience have revealed the interior to be a complex and dynamic place with myriad connections to the surface we inhabit, but the relationship isn’t mutual. We depend on the interior more than it depends on us.

While we’ve known about many of these vital interactions between surface and depth for decades, it’s only relatively recently that geoscientists have begun to trace the connections in any detail. High-pressure experiments heated with lasers plumb how water may have partitioned between the core and the rest of the planet after its formation. Super-deep diamonds return actual samples of minerals from as far down as the lower mantle, including physical evidence of sediments subducted from far above. Millions of seismic readings from thousands of earthquakes map the three-dimensional structure of the entire mantle, capturing unexpected complexity from downgoing slabs to plumes of heat rising from the edge of the core. These feed increasingly sophisticated models of how material convects in the mantle over hundreds of millions of years, constrained by reconstructions of the movement of tectonic plates on the surface. Even the solid inner core has been shown to be full of seismic variation, connected in enigmatic ways to the cooling history of Earth and the planet’s magnetic field. Each of these new windows into the deep helps to reveal the reality of all that is going on underneath the Anthropocene, and its relevance to the surface.

These links are multifarious, and not entirely understood, but some are so important it’s difficult to imagine our planet without them. One is the geodynamo: this flow of molten iron in the liquid outer core generates Earth’s magnetic field. This protects us and all life on the surface from the solar winds and other cosmic radiation, which would otherwise strip oxygen and water away from the atmosphere. That the geodynamo may be important for life on Earth is a longstanding idea. But researchers are beginning to uncover specific connections between the field and the evolution of Earth’s surface environment.

One recent study by the geophysicist Weijia Kuang at NASA and his colleagues points out a correlation between the strength of Earth’s magnetic field and levels of atmospheric oxygen over the past 540 million years: the stronger the field, the higher the concentration of oxygen. The reason for this link is mysterious. One possibility the researchers consider is that the stronger field reduces the loss of oxygen from the top of the atmosphere to space. Another idea is that they are linked by a third factor that affects both at once, such as the formation and breakup of supercontinents. This could influence the geodynamo by changing the flow of heat in the mantle while also influencing the geochemical cycles on the surface that control oxygen. Whatever the reason for this unexpected correlation, however, it points to a connection between the deepest parts of the planet and something as essential as the air we breathe.

The Earth system should be seen in full, linking the power of the deep planet with the vitality of the surface

Another connection is rock weathering, sometimes called Earth’s ‘global thermostat’. It works like this: as rocks erode, they can react with CO2 in the atmosphere, capturing the carbon in mineral form. Much of that carbon flows out into the oceans, where it piles up in sediments. These are eventually subducted into the mantle with the rest of the oceanic crust. This downward flow of carbon is balanced by volcanoes releasing much of the carbon into the atmosphere again as CO2. While weathering happens on the surface, it represents a deeper chemical exchange. The ‘weatherability’ of rocks is directly related to the depth of their origins in the interior, which lies out of chemical equilibrium with the atmosphere. This is why ‘enhanced rock weathering’ projects – which involve spreading crushed rock over land to speed up CO2 removal – use volcanic rocks.

This deep carbon cycle is what has maintained Earth’s relative climatological stability over most of its history, including taking down the temperature after catastrophic eruptions and helping escape ‘snowball Earth’ periods where the planet was locked in ice. Our current and fast-receding ‘icehouse’ climate owes its existence to this balance. A 2025 study by Benjamin Mills at the University of Leeds and his colleagues found cooling the planet enough to form icecaps required both a substantial contribution from rock weathering and a decline in the volume of CO2 released by volcanoes.

Plate tectonics itself, driven by the convective flow of heat in the mantle, much of it produced by the decay of radioactive elements in deep rocks, is thought to be a central pillar of Earth’s habitability. This interaction between the surface and the interior ensures a regular geochemical exchange. As well as serving as the thermostat described above, keeping CO2 in check, this constant cycling keeps the oceans from becoming too salty as more rock is eroded into them, and as they evaporate. The movement of tectonic plates also drives large-scale biological change that expands the diversity of organisms on the surface. At an even more fundamental level, tectonics builds continents among the oceans, enabling all life that depends on dry land, and thus the development of technologies like fire. The geodynamicists Taras Gerya and Robert Stern recently argued that Earth’s distinctive style of plate tectonics is likely to make this planet unique as a host of technological civilisation in the Solar System, and perhaps even in the galaxy. They are working to develop these ideas in a new field they call ‘biogeodynamics’, which aims to trace in detail the connections between the deep, slow cycles of the solid Earth and the faster cycles of the climate and living biosphere.

In their classic book How to Build a Habitable Planet (1984), the geologists Charles Langmuir and Wallace Broecker sum up this view that the interior is not a remote, separate part of Earth, but something integral to it. ‘Atmosphere, ocean, ocean crust, mantle, core, continents, and plate tectonics form a linked system that sustains the conditions of our habitable planet,’ they write. Now we’re talking. This is how the Earth system should be seen in full, linking the power of the deep planet with the vitality of the surface.

In the name of trying to limit our environmental impacts, invocations of the Anthropocene tend to imply that humans are Earth’s main protagonist. But we shouldn’t let this exaggerate our importance for the whole Earth system, adding once more to the hubris that got us into this predicament in the first place. By orienting ourselves towards the impassive and interminable movements of the deep Earth, we can bury the version of the Anthropocene in which we see ourselves at the centre of everything.

A few months ago, I came face-to-face with the way our world is shaped and supported by the deep Earth. This encounter came on a hiking trip with some friends up to the still-glaciated summit of Cotopaxi – a nearly 6,000-metre volcano in Ecuador. The mountain is one of the parade of huge volcanoes that line the Andean cordillera. In Indigenous Quechua stories and in local culture, these volcanoes are personified as deities called apus who are related to one another. In one story, the ‘male’ volcanos Taita (or Father) Cotopaxi and Taita Chimborazo compete for the admiration of the nearby ‘female’ volcano Mama Tungurahua. For Ecuadorians, these mountains are sources of dangerous eruptions and earthquakes. Yet they are also primary sources of water and fertile soil for the valley, and so are revered.

While I can’t speak to the existence of jealous romances among volcanoes, the idea that they are related to one another is absolutely true. All these volcanoes, both active and dormant, owe their existence to the deep cycles that link the surface and the interior – they are grand monuments to the hidden role of the deep Earth in our upper-world lives.

I had a glimpse of the Earth drawing on all its elemental spheres to rebuild itself

Unlike the volcanoes in Hawai‘i or Iceland, which are mainly powered by plumes of mantle heat rising from the edge of the core, the volcanoes of South America are powered by the interaction between the atmosphere, the oceans and the solid Earth. They occur above the subduction zone where the Nazca plate is descending beneath the continent. As the descending slab of oceanic crust rises in temperature, it releases the water and other volatiles like CO2 that have permeated its rocks over the tens of millions of years since it formed at the mid-ocean ridge. Many of these volatiles steam out of the thick marine sediments that cover it – including the rocks of continents eroded by weather, and the carboniferous bodies of innumerable organisms snowed down from the water column. As these volatile compounds rise into the wedge of solid mantle rock above the slab, they reduce the melting temperature within the rock. This generates low-density magmas that surge buoyantly to the surface and erupt.

When we reached the Cotopaxi summit after hiking through the night, the crater was fuming with sulphurous white steam that warmed the air; it last erupted in 2023. Chimborazo and Tungurahua poked out of the clouds on the horizon, catching the first sunlight. Far below us, the morning lights of Quito sprawled across the valley, its more than 2 million inhabitants living everywhere the volcanoes and steep slopes allowed. Taita Cotopaxi, prone to explosive eruptions, was surrounded by an open ring of fresh ashy rock called tuff, with páramo grassland just starting to take root after the last eruption. People knew not to live too directly in its embrace.

This scene brought me unexpectedly to tears. Standing on new land, built in part of sediments of the ocean drawn deep into the planet and disgorged again, it was a glimpse of the Earth drawing on all its elemental spheres – atmo-, hydro-, litho-, bio- – to rebuild itself. Maybe it was just the low oxygen, but I was struck by an overwhelming sense of gratitude at the chance to see it. In a breathless and extremely windy voice recording I made at the summit, I called the crater an ‘endless cathedral of renewal’. Listening back, it sounds a bit dramatic, but this is how it felt atop the mountain. It was as though the deep Earth had raised us up on this apu, high above the clouds, so that we might see what is central to this planet, and what is only passing over the surface.
